title: Growing pea shoots
subtitle: Sweet, tendril-bearing shoots from pre-soaked pea seed, cut in 10 to 14 days
excerpt: Pea shoots are one of the most popular microgreen crops: sweet, tender, and fast-growing once the large seed has been pre-soaked. Sow in a deep 25 cm tray after an 8-hour soak, blackout for three days, then light for 7 to 11 more days before cutting.
sourceNotes: UMass Extension microgreens guides (open-access). Cornell Cooperative Extension indoor growing material. Standard microgreen-growing practice synthesised from extension service material and widely-taught pea shoot methods.

glossaryTerms.definition: Soaking large, hard-coated seeds (peas, sunflowers, beans) in room-temperature water for 6 to 12 hours before sowing. The water penetrates the seed coat, triggers the germination signal, and dramatically reduces the time to the first visible shoot.

Watering by setting the growing tray inside a second tray filled with water, allowing the growing medium to draw moisture up from below. Keeps the seedling surface dry and reduces mould and damping-off risk in microgreen trays.

content.text: Pea shoots are a year-round indoor tray crop with a 10 to 14 day cycle. The large pea seed requires a pre-soak before sowing; without it, germination is slow and uneven. Sow on a 25 cm tray after an 8-hour water soak, blackout for three days, then move to light until the shoots are 8 to 12 cm tall and the first tendrils are developing. The flavour is sweet and grassy, the texture soft.

Pea shoots can be cut once and the tray will often produce a second cut from the same roots (lower yield, slightly coarser texture). Most growers take a single cut and start a fresh tray for the second harvest.

Light: a bright south-facing windowsill in spring and summer. In winter, a grow light 15 to 20 cm above the tray at 14 to 16 hours per day produces taller, more even shoots. Pea shoots in low winter light grow more slowly and lean strongly toward the light source; rotate the tray daily to counteract this.
Temperature: 16 to 22°C. Peas are the most cold-tolerant of the common microgreen crops; they germinate and grow reasonably even at 14°C, though the cycle extends to 16 to 18 days at the lower end.
the pea seed in room-temperature water for 8 to 12 hours. The seeds absorb water and the outer coat softens; they swell noticeably. Drain and rinse before sowing.

Day 0: sow. Fill a 25 cm tray with pre-dampened seed compost to within 2 cm of the rim (deeper than for small seeds, to support the larger root system). Spread the soaked seeds in a single dense layer, touching but not stacked. Do not cover with soil. Pea seeds are large enough to self-support on the surface.

Days 1 to 3: blackout. Cover with a second tray, weighted with something flat. The weight is particularly useful for peas, as the large seeds push up vigorously and can lift a light cover. Remove when the majority of shoots are upright and 3 to 4 cm tall.
Day 4 onward: light. Shoots green up rapidly in bright light.

daily: set the tray inside a second outer tray with 1 to 2 cm of water. Pea shoots use more water than brassica microgreens because of their size; check the medium daily and do not allow it to dry out.

Days 10 to 14: cut. When shoots are 8 to 12 cm tall and the first curling tendrils appear, cut 2 to 3 cm above the medium surface with scissors. Cut higher than brassicas to get the tender shoot tip without the tougher base. Rinse, use fresh or refrigerate for up to two days.

attrs.heading: Troubleshooting
attrs.intro: Common problems on pea shoot trays.

items.symptom: Slow germination despite soaking, most seeds fail to sprout after day 4
items.cause: Old seed stock, insufficient soak time, or cold room.
items.fix: Use fresh pea seed; older pea seed loses viability quickly. Soak for a full 8 to 12 hours in room-temperature water. Check the ambient temperature is above 15°C.

items.symptom: Mould on unsoaked or slow-germinating seeds after day 2
items.cause: Seeds sitting on a damp surface in warmth without germinating, allowing mould to colonise the seed coat.
items.fix: Use fresh seed. Rinse the soaked seeds thoroughly before sowing to remove the surface sugars that encourage mould. Better airflow helps.

items.symptom: Shoots lean strongly to one side
items.cause: Single-direction light source, common on a windowsill.
items.fix: Rotate the tray 180 degrees every day. A grow light positioned directly above the tray eliminates the problem.

items.symptom: Yellowing shoots after the first cut
items.cause: The roots have used up the energy reserves in the remaining stub.
items.fix: Pea shoots can produce a second cut but at noticeably lower quality. For consistent results, start a fresh tray rather than relying on regrowth.

content.text: Use untreated pea seed. Standard vegetable pea seed sold for outdoor growing is usually untreated but check the packet; some varieties carry a fungicide coating. Microgreen suppliers sell untreated pea seed in larger packs suited to tray growing. Garden pea, sugar snap, and snow pea varieties all work as pea shoot crops; garden pea produces the sweetest shoots.
